questions.title: Basic Method Overriding
questions.question: Create a base class Animal with a method speak(), and derive a subclass Dog that overrides speak() to output 'Woof'.
questions.explanation: Inheritance establishes an 'is-a' relationship between a superclass and a subclass using the extends keyword. When a subclass defines an instance method with the exact same name, return type, and parameter signature as a method in its superclass, it overrides that method. At runtime, the JVM uses dynamic method dispatch (invokevirtual): it inspects the actual object type on the heap rather than the reference variable's compile-time type. When speak() is invoked on a Dog instance, the JVM executes Dog's implementation, printing 'Woof'.
hints: Declare class Animal containing public void speak().
Declare class Dog extends Animal and override speak().
Instantiate Dog and invoke speak() to verify polymorphic dispatch.
questions.expectedOutput: Woof

questions.title: Subclass State and Behavior Extension
questions.question: Implement a Vehicle base class and a Car subclass that extends it by adding an additional field doors and a specialized method drive().
questions.explanation: Inheritance enables code reuse and structural specialization. When Car extends Vehicle, it inherits all non-private fields and methods from Vehicle while adding child-specific state and behavior. The subclass constructor uses super(brand) to initialize the inherited base fields before initializing its own doors field. In heap memory, a Car object contains storage for both the inherited brand field and the new doors field. Callers can invoke both inherited methods (start()) and subclass-specific methods (drive()) on the Car instance.
hints: Create Vehicle with protected String brand; and a start() method.
Extend it with class Car extends Vehicle adding private int doors;.
Add a drive() method in Car and demonstrate calling both start() and drive().
questions.expectedOutput:
Vehicle started: Toyota
Driving Toyota with 4 doors

questions.title: Super Method Invocation
questions.question: Call a parent class method from an overriding subclass method using super.methodName() to augment rather than completely replace base behavior.
questions.explanation: When a subclass overrides a parent method, the parent's original implementation is shadowed within the subclass instance. To extend the parent's logic rather than completely replacing it, the subclass uses super.methodName(). The super keyword tells the compiler to emit an invokespecial instruction that bypasses dynamic virtual dispatch and directly invokes the superclass implementation. This pattern is commonly used in lifecycle hooks, GUI rendering pipelines, and event listeners where child classes add custom logic while preserving necessary base processing.
hints: In Parent, write public void display() { System.out.println("Parent display"); }.
In Child extends Parent, override display() and invoke super.display(); first.
Add child-specific print statements immediately following the super invocation.
questions.expectedOutput:
Base system configured
Subsystem extensions active

questions.title: Compile-Time Override Verification
questions.question: Demonstrate the safety provided by the @Override annotation by overriding a method, and document in comments how typos in method names cause compilation failures.
questions.explanation: The @Override annotation is an optional but critical compile-time check in Java. When applied to a method, it instructs the compiler to verify that a method with the exact same signature exists in an accessible superclass or super-interface. If a developer introduces a typographical error (such as spek() instead of speak()) or alters a parameter type, the compiler raises an error: 'method does not override or implement a method from a supertype'. Without @Override, the compiler would treat the misspelled method as an entirely new overloaded method, causing subtle bugs at runtime when dynamic dispatch fails to invoke it.
hints: Annotate the subclass method with @Override.
Show a working override of process().
Add a comment explaining that misspelling the name as proces() triggers a compile error when @Override is present.
questions.expectedOutput: Customized processing executed

questions.title: Hierarchical ToString Extension
questions.question: Create a Person superclass and a Student subclass that adds a studentId field, overriding toString() in Student to incorporate super.toString().
questions.explanation: Extending string representations across an inheritance chain demonstrates cumulative state formatting. The Person superclass encapsulates base attributes (name, age) and formats them in its toString() method. The Student subclass adds studentId. When overriding toString() in Student, writing super.toString() + ", StudentID: " + studentId reuses the parent class's formatting logic instead of re-accessing private parent fields. This maintains encapsulation while producing a complete string representation of the combined object state.
hints: Implement toString() in Person returning "Name: " + name + ", Age: " + age.
In Student, call super.toString() inside its overridden toString().
Append ", StudentID: " + studentId to the superclass string result.
questions.expectedOutput: Name: Akshat, Age: 26, StudentID: STU-9921

questions.title: Single Inheritance Extension
questions.question: Demonstrate single class inheritance by extending an Animal class with a Cat subclass that overrides makeSound().
questions.explanation: Java supports single class inheritance: a class can directly extend exactly one superclass (class Sub extends Super). This design avoids the multiple inheritance diamond problem found in languages like C++. When Cat extends Animal, it forms a direct parent-child lineage. Calling cat.makeSound() uses virtual dispatch to invoke the overridden method in Cat. Single inheritance establishes clear, linear class hierarchies where responsibilities and state flow down a single chain.
hints: Define class Animal with a default makeSound() method.
Extend it with class Cat extends Animal and override makeSound() to print 'Meow'.
Instantiate Cat and execute makeSound().
questions.expectedOutput: Meow

questions.title: Dynamic Method Dispatch (Polymorphism)
questions.question: Store instances of Circle, Square, and Triangle in a Shape[] array. Iterate over the array and call draw() to observe dynamic method dispatch.
questions.explanation: Polymorphism enables treating objects of different subclasses uniformly through a shared superclass reference. When Circle, Square, and Triangle are stored in an array of type Shape[], their concrete types are upcast to Shape. In the iteration loop for (Shape s : shapes), calling s.draw() emits an invokevirtual bytecode instruction. At runtime, the JVM looks up the target object's virtual method table (vtable) and dispatches to the overridden method of the concrete subclass (Circle.draw(), Square.draw(), etc.). This allows client code to process collections of related objects without knowing their concrete types upfront.
hints: Create an array Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(), new Square(), new Triangle() };.
Ensure Circle, Square, and Triangle each override public void draw().
Use an enhanced for-each loop to invoke draw() on each element.
questions.expectedOutput:
Drawing Circle
Drawing Square
Drawing Triangle

questions.title: Instanceof Type Verification
questions.question: Iterate through an array of Shape references holding mixed subclasses, use instanceof to identify specific subtypes, and downcast safely to call subclass-specific methods.
questions.explanation: When working with polymorphic collections, elements are often upcast to their common supertype. Calling subclass-specific methods that are not declared in the superclass requires downcasting. Because downcasting an incompatible type throws a ClassCastException at runtime, the code must check the object's type first using the instanceof operator. If s instanceof Circle evaluates to true, the reference can be safely cast via (Circle) s to invoke subclass-specific methods like roll().
hints: Iterate over the array using a for-each loop.
Check types using if (shape instanceof Circle).
Explicitly cast Circle c = (Circle) shape; and call its specialized method.
questions.expectedOutput:
Circle rolling
Square sliding

questions.title: Final Class and Final Method Protection
questions.question: Demonstrate that declaring a class final prevents inheritance, and declaring a method final prevents subclasses from overriding it, documenting compiler restrictions in comments.
questions.explanation: The final keyword allows developers to restrict extension in object-oriented hierarchies. When a class is declared final, it cannot be extended by any subclass (cannot inherit from final class). This is standard for immutable classes like java.lang.String and java.lang.Integer to preserve immutability guarantees. When an individual method is marked final, subclasses can inherit and call it, but cannot override it (overridden method is final). This ensures critical algorithms and security validations cannot be modified or bypassed by subclasses.
hints: Mark a base class method public final void verifyToken().
Demonstrate that subclasses can invoke verifyToken() directly.
Explain in comments that attempting to extend a final class or override a final method fails compilation.
questions.expectedOutput:
Security token verified cryptographically
Task execution completed

questions.title: Multilevel Inheritance Method Aggregation
questions.question: Implement a 3-level inheritance hierarchy (A -> B -> C) where each level adds a distinct method, and demonstrate invoking all three methods on an instance of class C.
questions.explanation: Multilevel inheritance forms an extended chain of class derivation (C extends B, and B extends A). In this structure, the most derived subclass inherits the cumulative methods and accessible state from all ancestors above it. When an instance of C is allocated on the heap, its memory layout includes storage for all inherited non-private fields across the chain. Calling methods declared in A, B, and C on the C instance executes smoothly because the compiler resolves all inherited public and protected methods down the derivation path.
hints: Define class A { void methodA() ... }.
Define class B extends A { void methodB() ... }.
Define class C extends B { void methodC() ... } and call all three methods from an instance of C.
questions.expectedOutput:
Method A executed
Method B executed
Method C executed

questions.title: Polymorphic Area Calculator
questions.question: Create an abstract or base Shape class with an area() method, implement subclasses Circle and Rectangle, store them in a Shape[] array, and compute total combined area.
questions.explanation: Polymorphic method execution allows processing collections of related objects through a shared base type. The base Shape class defines double area(), which subclasses Circle (using PI * r * r) and Rectangle (using w * h) override with their specific formulas. When iterating over a Shape[] array, calling shape.area() uses virtual dispatch to invoke each object's concrete implementation. This allows calculating aggregate totals across mixed geometries without checking specific types or casting.
hints: Declare double area() in base class Shape.
In Circle, calculate Math.PI * radius * radius.
In Rectangle, calculate length * width.
questions.expectedOutput: Total Area: 24.57

questions.title: Polymorphic Payroll Processing
questions.question: Implement an Employee base class with Manager and Developer subclasses that override calculateSalary(), and compute payroll by iterating over an Employee[] array.
questions.explanation: Polymorphism simplifies business domain processing across organizational hierarchies. The Employee base class defines a baseline compensation calculation. The Manager subclass overrides it to add an executive bonus, while Developer overrides it to include project allowances. Storing diverse workers in an Employee[] array allows a payroll loop to invoke e.calculateSalary() uniformly. Dynamic dispatch routes each call to the appropriate calculation based on the employee's role, illustrating clean object-oriented architecture without procedural type checking.
hints: Base class Employee defines public double calculateSalary().
Subclasses Manager and Developer override calculateSalary() to apply role-specific bonuses.
Iterate over an Employee[] array to calculate and print the total payroll amount.
questions.expectedOutput: Total Payroll: $16500

questions.title: Field Hiding vs Method Overriding Disparity
questions.question: Declare a field with the same name in both parent and child classes, and demonstrate that field access resolves at compile time by reference type while method calls resolve at runtime by object type.
questions.explanation: In Java, fields do not participate in polymorphism; only non-private, non-static instance methods are overridden dynamically. When a child class declares a field with the exact same name as an accessible field in its parent class, it hides the parent field rather than overriding it. When accessing ref.title on a Parent ref = new Child() reference, the compiler resolves the field based on the declared compile-time reference type (Parent), reading the parent's field. Calling an overridden method ref.getTitle(), however, uses runtime virtual dispatch to execute the child's method.
hints: Declare public String title = "ParentTitle"; in Parent and public String title = "ChildTitle"; in Child.
Override a getTitle() method in both classes.
Access both ref.title and ref.getTitle() through a Parent ref = new Child() reference to observe the difference.
questions.expectedOutput:
Field access via reference (static binding):  ParentTitle
Method call via reference (dynamic dispatch): ChildTitle

questions.title: Protected State Access and ToString Chaining
questions.question: Implement a Vehicle class with protected fields make and speed, extend it with Car, and demonstrate direct protected access and super.toString() chaining.
questions.explanation: Protected member access allows subclasses to access internal state directly without going through public accessors. When Vehicle declares protected String make; and protected int speed;, subclass Car can read and modify those fields directly using this.make or make. In Car's toString() method, calling super.toString() reuses the parent class's base formatting, appending its own attributes (doors) to construct a complete description. This pattern maintains clean class boundaries while avoiding code duplication across inheritance tiers.
hints: Declare fields as protected in Vehicle.
Directly read those protected fields inside methods in Car extends Vehicle.
Chain string representations: return super.toString() + ", Doors: " + doors;.
questions.expectedOutput: Make: Honda, Speed: 120 km/h, Doors: 4

questions.title: Covariant Return Types
questions.question: Implement parent and child producer classes where the subclass overrides a factory method and narrows the return type to a more specific subtype (covariant return).
questions.explanation: Introduced in Java 5, covariant return types allow an overriding subclass method to declare a return type that is a subtype of the return type declared in the parent method. For example, if Producer.create() returns Item, subclass SpecializedProducer.create() can return SpecializedItem. This satisfies the Liskov Substitution Principle because SpecializedItem is an Item. Callers using the specific subclass reference receive the narrower type directly without needing an explicit cast, improving type safety and API usability.
hints: Create an Item class and a SpecializedItem extends Item subclass.
In Factory, declare public Item create().
In TechFactory extends Factory, override with public SpecializedItem create().
questions.expectedOutput:
Specialized Tech Item
Tech item configured

questions.title: Equals and HashCode Symmetry in Inheritance
questions.question: Demonstrate the symmetry violation that occurs when overriding equals() in subclasses using instanceof, and fix it using getClass() or composition.
questions.explanation: The equals() contract mandates symmetry: x.equals(y) must return true if and only if y.equals(x) returns true (Joshua Bloch, Effective Java). When extending a concrete class with new state fields (such as ColoredPoint adding a color to Point), implementing equals() using instanceof breaks symmetry. When evaluating point.equals(coloredPoint), point checks coordinates and returns true. However, evaluating coloredPoint.equals(point) checks color, finds it missing, and returns false. Using getClass() ensures that objects are equal only if they share the exact same runtime class, preserving symmetry across the hierarchy.
hints: Define Point with x, y and ColoredPoint extends Point adding color.
Show how instanceof causes p.equals(cp) to return true while cp.equals(p) returns false.
Fix the comparison in equals() using if (obj == null || getClass() != obj.getClass()) return false;.
questions.expectedOutput:
p.equals(cp):  false
cp.equals(p):  false
Symmetry preserved: true

questions.title: Pattern Matching for Instanceof
questions.question: Refactor a legacy block of if (obj instanceof Employee) { Employee e = (Employee) obj; ... } using modern pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16+).
questions.explanation: Introduced in Java 16 (JEP 394), pattern matching for instanceof simplifies type testing and downcasting into a single step. In legacy Java, developers had to check the type with instanceof and then write a separate explicit cast statement (Employee e = (Employee) obj;). Pattern matching combines these operations: if (obj instanceof Employee e) checks the type, and if true, automatically casts and binds the value to the scoped pattern variable e. This eliminates redundant casting code and reduces the risk of casting errors.
hints: Replace explicit casts with pattern syntax: if (emp instanceof Manager m).
Use the bound pattern variable m directly inside the conditional block.
Combine pattern variables with logical conditions, such as if (obj instanceof Manager m && m.hasBonus()).
questions.expectedOutput:
Manager of team size: 8
Standard: Employee

questions.title: Variable Shadowing vs Method Overriding
questions.question: Create parent and child classes with the same field name int value. Access the field through parent and child references to demonstrate that fields are not polymorphic.
questions.explanation: Polymorphic method dispatch does not apply to member fields in Java. When a child class declares an instance variable with the same identifier as a field in its superclass, the child field shadows the parent field. Both fields exist independently within the object on the heap. The field that gets accessed is resolved at compile time based strictly on the declared type of the reference variable (ref.value). In contrast, instance methods resolve dynamically at runtime based on the actual object instance on the heap.
hints: Declare public int value = 10; in Parent and public int value = 20; in Child.
Declare public int getValue() in both classes, returning their respective fields.
Compare ref.value with ref.getValue() on a Parent ref = new Child() reference.
questions.expectedOutput:
Field access (compile-time type Parent): 10
Method access (runtime dynamic dispatch): 20

questions.title: Composition over Inheritance Refactoring
questions.question: Refactor a design where Stack incorrectly inherits from ArrayList to use composition (delegation) instead, explaining the architectural benefits.
questions.explanation: The principle of 'Composition over Inheritance' states that classes should achieve polymorphic behavior and code reuse by wrapping component objects rather than inheriting implementation. When a class like Stack extends ArrayList, it exposes unintended list operations (add(index, elem), remove(index)) that break LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) stack invariants. Refactoring to composition wraps a private ArrayList inside Stack. The stack exposes only proper LIFO methods (push, pop, peek), delegating internally to the list while preventing arbitrary index access.
hints: Replace class Stack extends ArrayList with a private field: private List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();.
Implement push(item) by calling list.add(item).
Implement pop() by calling list.remove(list.size() - 1) to enforce LIFO semantics.
questions.expectedOutput:
Popped top element: 20
Peeked current top: 10

questions.title: Instanceof Pattern Matching in Polymorphic Hierarchies
questions.question: Use Java 16+ pattern matching for instanceof with guarded logic to process a heterogeneous Shape array, invoking specialized subclass methods cleanly.
questions.explanation: Pattern matching for instanceof simplifies processing heterogeneous object hierarchies by combining type verification, casting, and conditional checking into a single expression. In an expression like if (shape instanceof Circle c && c.getRadius() > 5.0), the compiler checks the type, binds the pattern variable c, and evaluates the second condition in one step. This eliminates boilerplate casting code and makes complex downcasting logic safer and more concise.
hints: Combine type binding with conditions: if (shape instanceof Circle c && c.getRadius() > 5).
Process Square with else if (shape instanceof Square sq).
Print specific diagnostic output from each matched branch.
questions.expectedOutput:
Large Circle detected, radius: 10.0
Small Circle detected, radius: 3.0
Square detected, side: 4.0

questions.title: Subclassing and Override Prohibition Guards
questions.question: Implement a security framework showing that declaring a class final prevents extension and declaring a method final prevents overriding, demonstrating how this protects sensitive code.
questions.explanation: Security-sensitive architectures use final modifiers to protect core invariants from being compromised via subclassing or method overriding. If a security class were extensible, a malicious or buggy subclass could override verification methods to bypass authentication checks or leak credentials. Marking the critical validation method final ensures that even if the class is extended, the validation logic cannot be replaced. Marking the entire class final prevents any subclassing whatsoever, ensuring that instances cannot be substituted by unauthorized subclasses.
hints: Declare a base AuthModule with public final boolean authenticate(String token).
Declare public final class SecureSession that cannot be extended.
Document in comments the compiler errors generated when attempting to extend or override these components.
questions.expectedOutput:
Authentication passed: true
Session created: SES-9921

questions.title: Subclass Equals Symmetry Breakdown and Fix
questions.question: Demonstrate the classic symmetry violation when overriding equals() in subclasses using instanceof, and resolve it using exact getClass() checks.
questions.explanation: The equals() contract requires symmetry: x.equals(y) must return true if and only if y.equals(x) returns true (Joshua Bloch, Effective Java). When extending a concrete class with new state fields, implementing equals() using instanceof breaks symmetry. For example, a Point(x, y) compared against a ColorPoint(x, y, color) will return true (since ColorPoint instanceof Point is true), but the reverse comparison returns false because Point lacks the color field. Using getClass() ensures that objects are considered equal only if they share the exact same concrete runtime class, preserving symmetry across the inheritance hierarchy.
hints: Show how instanceof causes p.equals(cp) to evaluate to true while cp.equals(p) evaluates to false.
Fix equals() in Point using if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;.
Verify in main that symmetry holds (p.equals(cp) == cp.equals(p)).
questions.expectedOutput:
p.equals(cp): false
cp.equals(p): false

questions.title: Stack API: Inheritance vs Composition
questions.question: Implement a Stack by extending ArrayList to show how unwanted methods leak into the public API, then refactor it using composition to provide a clean, encapsulated stack interface.
questions.explanation: Extending a collection class like ArrayList to implement a Stack violates proper interface segregation. Because inheritance exposes all public methods of the superclass, a Stack extends ArrayList inherits methods like add(index, element), remove(index), and set(index, element). These methods allow callers to insert or delete elements in the middle of the stack, breaking the LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) stack invariant. Using composition wraps an ArrayList as a private internal field instead. The class exposes only proper stack operations (push, pop, peek), delegating to the internal list while preventing arbitrary index access.
hints: Show that inheriting from ArrayList allows invalid calls like stack.add(0, 999) that bypass LIFO rules.
Refactor to composition with a private field: private List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();.
Expose only push(), pop(), and peek() methods in the refactored class.
questions.expectedOutput:
Popped top element: 20
Peeked current top: 10

questions.title: Covariant Return Types with Deep Cloning
questions.question: Implement a cloning hierarchy where Parent.copy() returns Parent and Child.copy() narrows its return type to Child, demonstrating covariant return types without downcasting.
questions.explanation: Covariant return types allow an overriding method in a subclass to return a more specific subtype than the method it overrides in the parent class. At the bytecode level, the compiler generates a synthetic bridge method to satisfy the parent class's signature while allowing callers using the subclass reference to receive the narrower type directly. When Child.copy() declares public Child copy(), callers can write Child cloned = c.copy() without needing an explicit cast (Child) c.copy(). This improves code readability and compile-time type safety.
hints: In Parent, define public Parent copy().
In Child extends Parent, override with public Child copy().
Demonstrate in main that invoking copy() on a Child reference requires no cast.
questions.expectedOutput: Cloned Child ID: 101 | Name: Akshat

questions.title: Liskov Substitution Principle Checker
questions.question: Demonstrate the classic Rectangle-Square LSP violation where Square extends Rectangle breaks resizing behavior, and refactor the class structure to ensure all subclasses can substitute their base types safely.
questions.explanation: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states that objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without breaking application correctness. In mathematics, a square is a rectangle, but modeling this with class Square extends Rectangle violates LSP in software. A rectangle allows setting width and height independently. In a Square subclass, setting width must also set height to maintain equal sides. If a method expects a Rectangle and resizes width and height independently to calculate area, passing a Square breaks the method's assumptions and produces incorrect results. The fix is to make Rectangle and Square separate classes implementing a common Shape interface.
hints: Demonstrate how setting width on a Square also mutates height, breaking rectangle expectations.
Refactor so both classes implement a common interface Shape with a getArea() method.
Verify that both shapes calculate area correctly without violating substitution expectations.
questions.expectedOutput:
Rectangle Area: 50
Square Area:    25

questions.title: Double Dispatch via Visitor Pattern
questions.question: Implement double dispatch using the Visitor pattern across an element hierarchy (TextElement, ImageElement) and a DocumentVisitor.
questions.explanation: Java supports single dispatch: method execution is determined dynamically by the runtime type of the target object (this), while method parameters are resolved at compile time based on their declared types. Double dispatch determines execution based on the runtime types of two objects: the receiver and the parameter. The Visitor pattern achieves this using two calls: 1) The client invokes element.accept(visitor) on an element hierarchy, which dynamically dispatches to the concrete element. 2) Inside that element, visitor.visit(this) is called, passing this as the concrete type to dispatch to the corresponding overloaded visitor method. This allows adding new operations across object hierarchies without modifying existing element classes.
hints: Define Element with void accept(Visitor v).
In TextElement, implement accept by calling v.visit(this).
Define Visitor with overloaded visit(TextElement) and visit(ImageElement) methods.
questions.expectedOutput:
Exporting text element
Exporting image element

questions.title: Virtual Table Dispatch Emulation
questions.question: Simulate the JVM vtable (virtual method table) mechanism in plain Java using function pointers/lambdas in a class hierarchy lookup map.
questions.explanation: To execute virtual method calls efficiently, the JVM uses an internal lookup structure called a virtual method table (vtable). Every class with virtual methods has a vtable containing pointers to the executable bytecode for each method. When a subclass overrides a method, its vtable entry points to the subclass implementation; inherited methods that are not overridden point to the superclass implementation. When invokevirtual executes, the JVM reads the method offset in the object's vtable and jumps to that address in O(1) time. Emulating this in Java using a Map<String, Runnable> illustrates how dynamic dispatch works under the hood.
hints: Create a base class that initializes a Map<String, Runnable> vtable.
Subclasses inherit the vtable and overwrite map entries for methods they override.
Simulate dispatch by looking up and executing methods by name from the map.
questions.expectedOutput: Child overridden vtable implementation

questions.title: Multiple Interface Default Method Collision
questions.question: Implement two interfaces with identical default methods in a single class. Write the overriding code to resolve the diamond collision using InterfaceName.super.method().
questions.explanation: With the introduction of default methods in Java 8, classes implementing multiple interfaces can encounter default method signature collisions (the diamond problem). If interface A and interface B both define a default method default void log(), a class implementing both interfaces fails to compile: 'class inherits unrelated defaults for log()'. The compiler cannot infer which default implementation to prefer. To resolve this ambiguity, the implementing class must explicitly override the conflicting method and specify which interface implementation to invoke using InterfaceName.super.method() (e.g., A.super.log()).
hints: Define interface Alpha { default void ping() { ... } } and interface Beta { default void ping() { ... } }.
In class ServiceNode implements Alpha, Beta, override ping() explicitly.
Choose an implementation using Alpha.super.ping(); or provide custom logic.
questions.expectedOutput:
Alpha default ping
ServiceNode custom ping

questions.title: Plugin Extension Framework
questions.question: Build an extensible plugin base class hierarchy where child plugins inherit lifecycle methods (init, execute, teardown) with polymorphic execution control.
questions.explanation: The Template Method pattern uses inheritance to define the overarching skeleton of an algorithm in a base class while letting subclasses override specific steps without changing the overall structure. The abstract base class Plugin declares a public final void run() template method that orchestrates the lifecycle sequence: init(), executeTask(), and teardown(). Marking run() as final ensures that subclasses cannot alter the execution sequence. Subclasses override the individual protected step methods to implement their custom behavior, demonstrating controlled inheritance in plugin framework architectures.
hints: Declare public final void run() in the abstract base class to enforce the execution sequence.
Define protected step methods: init(), executeTask(), and teardown().
Extend the base class in DatabasePlugin and demonstrate running the complete lifecycle.
questions.expectedOutput:
Plugin initialized
Executing database synchronization task
Plugin cleaned up
